item.content:encoded: Last week, I started a discussion of General Yakubu Gowon’s multi-themed memoirs, My Life of Duty & Allegiance. My focus was on the book’s general tone, which I find unduly self-justificatory. In his attempts to defend his legacy, General Gowon presents himself as a saintly figure who did no wrong as a leader, whereas some introspection and nuanced reflection would have helped. That said, the book is a treasure trove of insightful details that enrich our historical narrative. This week, I will focus on one of such insights, namely, the quality of governance and public service ethos under General Gowon’s regime, with Chief Obafemi Awolowo singled out as the arrowhead of a remarkable governance approach that, if replicated today, would transform how Nigeria is governed and, thus, this country’s fortunes. As a political economist and policy practitioner who spent nearly 20 years advising the UK government on diverse policy areas, in addition to teaching public policy, I have professional and intellectual interests in how government is run. Thus, I was enthralled by General Gowon’s fascinating accounts of how the affairs of state were conducted under his administration, with the triumvirate of politicians (as ministers), civil servants (as technocrats), and universities and think-tanks (as sounding boards) driving policy formulation and implementation and setting standards of good and effective governance. Sitting atop the triumvirate was Chief Awolowo, an extraordinarily transformative leader! Indeed, if General Gowon’s memoirs can be said to have a hero, that hero is Chief Obafemi Awolowo, appointed by Gowon as the Vice Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, and Commissioner of Finance in his administration. In every reference to Chief Awolowo in the memoirs, General Gowon writes glowingly and superlatively about him. Gowon also gives credit to his colleagues in the Supreme Military Council, SMC, and the first-class mandarins who ran the civil service for his administration’s successes, especially its ability to prosecute a 30-month civil war “without endangering the national economy”. But he reserves his most generous praise for Chief Awolowo. Hear Gowon: “Chief Awolowo’s business acumen, political sagacity, economic wizardry and thorough man-management ability would later prove quite useful and helpful in ensuring that we kept our finances intact during and immediately after the civil war that broke out a few weeks after his appointment to the FEC.” He adds: “Without any argument, he made invaluable contributions.” Of course, Chief Awolowo’s reputation preceded him. As the premier of the Western Region, he performed so superbly that Harold Wilson, then British prime minister, described him as a “world-class leader”, who would make an outstanding President of America or Prime Minister of Britain. General Gowon himself referenced Chief Awolowo’s pedigree, saying that he appointed him as the Commissioner of Finance with concurrent responsibility as Vice-Chairman of the FEC “because of his experience in politics and management of the economy of the old Western Region.” Indeed, General Gowon was so enamoured of Chief Awolowo that he admits in his memoirs that one of his administration’s flagship policies, the Universal Primary Education, UPE, was based on a policy introduced by Chief Awolowo as premier. “In scope and content,” Gowon writes, “UPE was not radically different from the model that was initiated by Chief Awolowo in the defunct Western Region while he was the Premier.” Two lessons emerge from this narrative. First, good leaders get the brightest and best in their teams; they form what a British prime minister described as GOATs (“Government of All the Talents”). Second, good leaders embrace good ideas and best practices worldwide. Indeed, one of the universally recognised approaches to sound policymaking is international comparison, which allows a government to consider what works elsewhere. Sadly, neither lesson is embedded in governance in Nigeria today. For instance, today, a Nigerian leader would fill his cabinet with cronies and political jobbers rather than seasoned technocrats and brilliant administrators. There’s also the phenomenon of policy discontinuities. Virtually every government won’t complete projects started by its predecessor, let alone copy sensible policies elsewhere, resulting in widespread abandoned projects and policy failures. But there’s another unlearned lesson. Chief Awolowo was never a yes-man in General Gowon’s government. Gowon himself cites two instances to prove this. In both instances, General Gowon eventually had his way, but Awolowo laid down the marker. In one case, General Gowon procured the services of a Lebanese contractor for the government. But Chief Awolowo refused to approve payment to the contractor, arguing that “the process of getting help from the Lebanese was not properly followed and documented and, as such, was an extra-budgetary expenditure.” Tell me, how many extra-budgetary expenditures are waived through without due process today? Can a finance minister challenge a president’s frivolous spending today? In another case, Chief Awolowo refused to approve a request for additional money for Gowon’s upkeep after the original budget was exhausted. He argued that the possibility of overshoots should have been considered before the budget was prepared and approved. This is how Gowon puts it in his memoirs: “Everyone knew how difficult it was to get anything out of Chief Awolowo without well-reasoned arguments.” What an extraordinary testimonial! But where are such principled and painstakingly meticulous ministers and public officers in Nigeria today? Sadly, none! To be sure, a tree does not make a forest, and Chief Awolowo did not act alone. As premier of the Western Region and later as Commissioner for Finance and Vice Chairman of the FEC, Chief Awolowo was surrounded by outstanding colleagues and civil servants. For instance, General Gowon mentions the sterling role of Professor Adebayo Adedeji, the world-renowned economist, who was the Commissioner for Economic Development. And talking about bureaucrats, who can forget the “Super Perm Secs” of the Gowon era? As the German sociologist and political economist Max Weber put it, “the state will not conduct its affairs without the bureaucracy.” Oxbridge-educated mandarins like Ahmed Joda, Allison Ayida and Philip Asiodu led what Gowon describes as “the deeply cerebral, committed and efficient technocrats in the civil service”, which he calls “the engine room” of his government. But where are today’s “super perm secs”? Where is today’s vibrant and technocratic civil service? Sadly, today, Nigeria has one of the worst civil services in the world, a subject I discuss in my book, In The National Interest, arguing that the collapse of the civil service and the public sector in general is at the heart of Nigeria’s acutely weak state capacity. As a scholar-practitioner, I was also excited about General Gowon’s accounts of how his government worked closely with universities. He writes: “We made exceptionally effective use of the many eggheads that populated the various university campuses to shape the policy directions.” He adds: “Many of the dons at the university were our formal and informal sounding boards for policy formulations and analyses.” In the UK, the government works in tandem with universities and think-tanks to shape policies. Sadly, in Nigeria, the government is anti-intellectual, with academics and think-tanks ostracised and treated as pariahs, rarely engaged in policy development. General Gowon makes another profound point about the policy process, saying: “These policies were not unilateral decisions. We diligently thought through the policies, and we implemented them based on their overall benefits to the people.” Compare that with how President Tinubu impulsively removed the fuel subsidy after he was “possessed by courage”,

item.description: By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do. Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. The better yesterday’s infrastructure becomes, the harder tomorrow’s infrastructure can be to adopt. Nigeria had a different incentive. Nigeria faced different circumstances. Card payments existed, but the country had stronger incentives to develop alternative digital rails. Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries. The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance. A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately. It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines. The CJN also used the occasion to launch the second edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual (JEM), which she said will help judicial officers locate relevant authorities, appreciate the development of the law and approach recurring issues with greater clarity. According to the CJN, by bringing together the relevant constitutional provisions, the Electoral Act 2026, applicable practice directions and judicial decisions, the Manual provides a useful resource for judicial officers and other stakeholders in the electoral adjudicatory process. She was quick to warn, however, that it should serve only as a guide and a reference tool. It does not replace independent judicial reasoning or relieve any judicial officer of the duty to consider each case on its own facts, the arguments of counsel and the applicable law. The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, said the early swearing-in of the tribunal judges was a clear demonstration of the judiciary’s commitment to ensuring that electoral disputes are handled promptly, competently and in accordance with the law. Fagbemi noted that election petition tribunals occupy a unique position in Nigeria’s democratic architecture, which is why the adjudication of electoral disputes continues to attract intense public attention and scrutiny. By providing the constitutional mechanism through which electoral grievances are peacefully resolved, he said, the tribunals are indispensable to political stability and public trust in the electoral process. The AGF drew attention to the far-reaching reforms introduced by the Electoral Act 2026, which he said aim to strengthen electoral transparency, promote internal party democracy, modernise electoral administration and redefine the framework for electoral disputes. The Act restricts judicial intervention in internal party affairs. Section 83(5) ousts the jurisdiction of the courts over disputes concerning the internal affairs of political parties, while Section 83(6) stipulates sanctions for intra-party litigation. The Act restricts interim and interlocutory injunctions in prohibited intra-party proceedings, provides for accelerated hearings, and prescribes minimum costs of N10 million each against the litigant and counsel. Likewise, Section 138(1) limits the grounds for election petitions. The amended law confines election petitions to corrupt practices, substantial non-compliance with electoral law, and failure to secure a majority of lawful votes. Significantly, it omits candidate disqualification as an express post-election ground, potentially shifting qualification disputes to pre-election proceedings. The AGF argued that the innovations in the amended Act represent a significant recalibration of Nigeria’s electoral framework ahead of the general elections. “Their ultimate transformative impact will depend on effective enforcement by INEC, compliance by political parties and judicial interpretation,” he added. For the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, electoral litigation has become increasingly complex. He observed that, beyond the familiar questions of voting, counting and collation, disputes now concern voter accreditation, electronic transmission of results, technological failures, the integrity of digital records, party primaries, candidate nominations and the conduct of election officials. He said the Electoral Act 2026 has provided the legislative framework for the forthcoming general elections. “Of particular relevance is Section 60(3), which addresses electronic transmission of polling-unit results and the legal implications of communication failures. “Its interpretation, alongside other provisions of the new Act, may feature prominently in future petitions. “The deployment of the BVAS and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) has brought greater technological sophistication to election administration and public access to electoral information. “At the same time, these systems raise questions about the authenticity, admissibility and probative value of electronic records, their relationship with physical documents, and the consequences of technical disruptions. “A clear distinction must be maintained between the generation of technological information, the statutory purpose it serves and the legal standard required to prove a case before a tribunal. “The distinction between pre-election matters and post-election petitions must be carefully observed,” the INEC Chairman added. Although INEC and the judiciary perform distinct but complementary constitutional functions, the credibility of the elections cannot be judged solely by the conduct of voting or the declaration of results. It will also depend on public confidence that electoral disputes will be determined independently, fairly and in accordance with the law. As the CJN pointed out, the 2027 elections will be a defining moment in the nation’s democratic journey. She warned that the courtroom must not become an extension of the political arena, stressing that disputes must be resolved on the basis of the pleadings, evidence and applicable law. Of the 375 judges nominated, 138 have previous tribunal experience, while 237 are new to such proceedings. The workshop is expected to have equipped them with the skills and knowledge to navigate the murky waters of election litigation and arrive at legally sound decisions. By fairly determining any disputes arising from the 2027 elections, the judiciary stands to safeguard the people’s mandate, uphold constitutional supremacy and sustain public confidence in democratic governance. item.title: Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship
item.description: By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty. April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office. He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life. “Tomorrow, sir,” I answered. That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso. When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. Beyond feeding my body, Mr. Omotoso fed my dreams. He encouraged me to keep studying while working and never once treated my academic ambitions as an inconvenience. During one management meeting, when questions were raised about my qualifications, he defended my potential and appealed for patience while I worked toward becoming a graduate. I was determined not to disappoint him. In 2014, I graduated from the then Lagos State Polytechnic with a Distinction. He celebrated the achievement, then immediately urged me to aim higher. With his continued support, I went on to Caleb University, Imota, Lagos, where I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science in 2019, graduating with Second Class Upper honours and a CGPA of 4.36. For someone who had started as an errand boy, this was more than academic progress. It was living proof that when someone believes in your potential, your circumstances need not determine your destination. Mr. Omotoso’s fatherly role extended far beyond the professional and academic. When I married in 2018, he provided a Honda Pilot and a personal driver to take me around all day, ensuring the occasion was memorable. On August 20, 2019, he was appointed Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. Before leaving The Nation, he ensured my contributions were recognised with a promotion to Web Officer. A month into his new assignment, he invited me to join him at the Ministry of Information and Strategy. That invitation opened yet another significant chapter in my career. Since then, I have had the privilege of serving closely with him as his Personal Assistant and Programme Analyst within the Lagos State Government. His commitment to my progress did not end there. He played an instrumental role in my appointment to the Lagos State Civil Service on December 31, 2024, personally presenting my credentials to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for consideration and approval. How does one adequately thank a man who has consistently opened doors, sometimes long before one even knew those doors existed? Yet my story is only one among countless testimonies of his compassion. Over the years, I have watched him discreetly pay hospital bills for people with whom he shares no family ties, sponsor the education of children whose parents could not afford school fees, and quietly rescue others from difficult circumstances. He does not need a camera to demonstrate kindness, nor does he wait for applause before helping others. Behind his serious editorial background and the demands of public office is also a man blessed with a remarkable sense of humour. An accomplished journalist, columnist and writer, Mr. Omotoso has a gift for satire. His humorous observations can turn even tense moments into shared laughter. And then there is table tennis. Anyone who has faced him across the table knows that losing is not exactly his favourite pastime. He approaches every game with the intensity of an editor scrutinising a controversial front-page headline. Every point matters, every rally is a battle, and every defeat deserves a detailed explanation. At 65, I suspect his opponents will still need more than youthful energy to defeat him. As I celebrate this remarkable man, I see far beyond the professional titles and accomplishments. I see a compassionate father figure, a bridge-builder, a generous leader, and a man whose quiet influence continues to transform lives. Sir, on your 65th birthday, I pray that Almighty God grants you long life, sound health, renewed strength, divine protection, and enduring peace. May the years ahead be filled with greater accomplishments, happiness, and the joy of seeing the many lives you have touched continue to flourish. May God reward every sacrifice you have made for others, replenish every resource you have so freely and generously shared, and surround you with love, honour and abundant blessings. May your pen never run dry, your wisdom never diminish, your laughter never cease, and may you continue winning your table tennis matches, even when your opponents believe they deserve a chance! For more than 22 years, I have experienced your kindness firsthand. I may never be able to repay all you have done for me, but I will forever remain grateful. Happy 65th birthday, my boss, my mentor, my father figure, and my God-sent benefactor. The world may know you as Gbenga Omotoso, the accomplished journalist and Commissioner. I know you as the man God used to rewrite the story of a fatherless boy. And for that, I will remain eternally grateful. •Uwemedimo is a Programme Analyst and Personal Assistant to the Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. item.title: Right-sizing the map of Africa
item.description: The United Nations General Assembly has, for the first time, formally endorsed a global shift away from the centuries-old Mercator map in favour of projections that show Africa—and other equatorial regions—in their true relative size. This “Correct the Map” resolution, spearheaded by Togo on behalf of the African Group and backed by the African Union, passed by 164 votes to one, with six abstentions. While non-binding, it marks a watershed moment in how the world visually represents the continent—and, by extension, how it perceives Africa’s weight in global affairs. The root of the misrepresentation lies in the Mercator projection, devised in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator for maritime navigation. To keep compass bearings straight, Mercator preserved angles and shapes—but at the cost of area. The result: landmasses near the poles, such as Europe, North America and Greenland, are visually enlarged, while those near the equator, including Africa, Latin America and South Asia, are shrunk. On typical Mercator wall maps, Greenland appears roughly the same size as Africa. In reality, Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, making it around 14 times larger than Greenland’s 2.1 million square kilometres. This is not a minor quirk; it is a systematic visual bias baked into the most widely used world map for nearly five centuries. The resolution encourages governments, schools, international organisations, media houses and technology companies to adopt equal-area projections, especially the Equal Earth projection, whenever comparative continental size matters. item.title: Spain coach optimistic over Yamal’s fitness for England Nations League clash
item.description: Spain coach Luis de la Fuente said Wednesday he is optimistic Barcelona winger Lamine Yamal will be fit to face England in the Nations League at the weekend. The 19-year-old winger will miss the world champions’ visit to face the Czech Republic in Prague on Thursday with a knee problem and is set to join up with Spain after that game. Yamal played for Barcelona in the 2-1 La Liga win over Atletico Madrid on Sunday and on Monday Spain said he would not travel to face the Czechs. “He got hurt in the last match, he had some discomfort in one knee, he went for the usual treatment, a scan in Barcelona, and they saw he had inflammation and fluid in the knee — that meant he needed rest,” De la Fuente told reporters. “Our medical staff and his medical staff have a fantastic relationship, and I decided that his trip here should be avoided without knowing whether he’d be in any condition to play.” The coach said he had spoken to the winger and his recovery was looking positive ahead of England’s visit to Madrid on Sunday. “He’s doing a series of exercises with his physio and with the club that indicate the recovery is going well,” continued De la Fuente. “We believe, I’m optimistic, that on Friday he’ll be with us.” De la Fuente dismissed the idea that Yamal, who came third in the Ballon d’Or voting in October, has any special privileges compared to his La Roja team-mates. “He has no privileges, and his team-mates are relaxed about it, because we treat everyone the same,” added the coach. “In similar situations we would have done exactly the same for any other player, and the players know that.” – Unstoppable run – Spain have won all four games so far in Group A3 and sealed qualification to the quarter-finals. The committee is expected to serve for six months. The appointment comes against the background of earlier disagreements over the party’s state leadership. It also arrives at a particularly sensitive moment for the ADC nationally. The Federal High Court’s November 5 judgment invalidating the David Mark-led national leadership has raised questions about the legal authority behind the party’s nominations. The party has appealed and applied for a stay of execution. However, no appellate reversal or granted stay has been confirmed. The Kano appointment must therefore be viewed in the context of both state-level organisational disagreements and the unresolved national leadership dispute. For now, the appointment establishes a new administrative arrangement. It does not settle every question about the party’s leadership or provide evidence of changing voter preferences. ADC: THE LEGAL BATTLE WIDENS The most consequential national development remains the dispute over the ADC’s leadership and nominations. On November 5, the Federal High Court invalidated decisions taken by the David Mark-led national executive, including the process that produced Atiku Abubakar as the party’s presidential candidate. The ADC rejected the judgment and subsequently filed an appeal and an application for a stay. Now the controversy has taken another turn. Candidates associated with the party have petitioned international diplomatic missions and organisations, including the United Nations, United States Embassy, British High Commission, European Union and ECOWAS. They are seeking attention to the legal and electoral implications of the judgment and have raised concerns about delays in obtaining its certified copy. The candidates say they intend to pursue lawful remedies. Their petition does not overturn the judgment. Nor does it amount to a stay of execution. And it does not establish that every ADC candidate has been finally excluded from the ballot. But it demonstrates that the dispute is no longer confined to the party’s national leadership. Candidates across different states now have a direct interest in the outcome. For the ADC, the immediate challenge is legal certainty. For INEC, the challenge is determining how to respond to the judgment and any subsequent appellate orders. And for the wider electoral process, the question is whether these disputes can be resolved sufficiently early to provide clarity for parties, candidates and voters. The legal status of a party’s nominations is not the same thing as its political support. That distinction must remain central to our Election Watch. Stella Charles Archibong, the party’s deputy governorship candidate, has withdrawn from the ticket and declared support for Governor Bassey Otu’s re-election campaign through the Back to South Movement. The withdrawal became public earlier in the week. NDC governorship candidate John Odey has acknowledged the development and indicated that consultations are continuing. This is different from an ordinary party supporter announcing a change of allegiance. Archibong was part of the governorship ticket itself. Her departure therefore raises immediate questions about the party’s replacement arrangements and the procedures required for recognition by INEC. No replacement has yet been independently verified on the Commission’s published list. For Cross River, the development concerns candidate organisation and nomination continuity. It does not establish how many voters, if any, will change their preferences because of her decision. OGUN: ADEBUTU’S CASE APPROACHES A DECISION A file photo of Ladi Adebutu. X@adiadebutu In Ogun State, the PDP’s governorship nomination dispute is approaching another important stage. The Federal High Court is scheduled to deliver judgment on Friday, November 13, in the case concerning Ladi Adebutu’s exclusion from INEC’s published governorship list. INEC maintains that Adebutu’s name was absent from the PDP membership register originally submitted to the Commission. In its court filings, the Commission says searches of the register identified Adebutu’s running mate but did not establish Adebutu’s inclusion. It also disputes membership documentation subsequently presented in support of his nomination. Adebutu and the PDP reject the basis of his exclusion. These are competing positions before the court. They should not be presented as judicial findings. The forthcoming judgment could determine the next stage of the dispute, although further appeals may remain possible. The political implications will depend on the court’s decision and any subsequent action by INEC. Until then, the party’s ballot-access position remains unresolved. item.title: Canada to fast-track permanent residence for 200,000 foreigners in 2027
item.description: The Canada government has announced plans to accelerate permanent residence (PR) processing for up to 200,000 foreign nationals already living in the country in 2027, as part of efforts to reduce immigration application backlogs and provide greater certainty for newcomers. item.title: US withdraws from U17 World Cup in Qatar over security fears
item.description: The United States has withdrawn from the upcoming Under-17 soccer World Cup in Qatar due to concerns about security in the Middle East, US media reported Wednesday. Players were informed of the decision just over a week before the tournament is due to begin on November 19, US Soccer Collective and The Athletic reported, citing anonymous sources. US Soccer, the sport’s governing body in the United States, did not immediately confirm the news or respond to AFP’s request for comment. The war in the Middle East began in February with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which retaliated by targeting, among others, Gulf countries allied with Washington. Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have been punctuated by repeated threats from the United States and Israel to resume bombardments of Iran. Multiple sporting events in the Middle East have been affected, including the tennis WTA Finals which were scheduled to be held in Saudi Arabia — which neighbors Qatar — but are instead now taking place at Indian Wells in the US. This season’s Formula One Grand Prix in Jeddah was cancelled, while the race in Bahrain was called off and later rescheduled under the same name in Malaysia. Several events in Saudi Arabia have also been cancelled or postponed in recent weeks following attacks on the country by the Houthis in Yemen. The US is one of 48 teams scheduled to play in the Under-17 World Cup, in a group with Montenegro, Chile and Algeria. The Under-17 World Cup shifted to an annual event last year, and is being held in Qatar for five consecutive years. Announcing its host decision in 2024, FIFA said the decision to choose a single host nation for multiple editions centered on the ability to make “use of existing footballing infrastructure in the interest of tournament efficiencies and sustainability”. Qatar was the venue for the 2022 men’s World Cup. Vanguard News The post US withdraws from U17 World Cup in Qatar over security fears appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Mbappe ruled out of France’s Nations League game against Italy
item.description: France’s captain Kylian Mbappe will miss his country’s Nations League match against Italy with a hamstring problem, coach Zinedine Zidane said Wednesday. Les Bleus take on Roberto Mancini’s Italy in Milan on Thursday as they bid to strengthen their grip on top spot in Group A1, before facing Turkey in Bordeaux on Sunday. “He will miss tomorrow, he felt a little pain and we won’t take any risk,” said Zidane. “It’s a shame to lose players but it’s part of the game. I hope that it’s nothing too serious and that he’ll be available for Sunday… It’s just a minor issue.” The Real Madrid forward is back in the France squad for this camp after missing their last three matches through injury. He has already netted 17 goals in all competitions for his club this season. Mbappe scored the winning goal in Zidane’s first match as coach, against Turkey in September in the Nations League, but had to leave the pitch shortly afterwards due to pain in his left knee. After three wins and a draw in four group games, victory over Italy would see France qualify for the quarter-finals. But over the course of my practice, I have become a bit more environmentally aware.” ﻿ Statistics cited by Green Network Asia indicate that over 200 million pairs of flip-flops are discarded each year globally, contributing significantly to plastic and rubber pollution in landfills and oceans.
